# Introduction

This is an R Markdown document. Markdown is a simple formatting syntax for authoring HTML, PDF, and MS Word documents. For more details on using R Markdown see http://rmarkdown.rstudio.com.

When you click the Knit button a document will be generated that includes both content as well as the output of any embedded R code chunks within the document. You can embed an R code chunk like this:

```{r}

# Summary is a built in function used to generate a statistic summary of a dataset.

# Here we need to get summary of cars dataset.

summary(cars)

```

Including Plots

You can also embed plots, for example:

```{r}
# Create temperature data
temperature <- seq(0, 360, by = 20)

# Create pressure data
pressure <- c(
  0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0,
  5, 10, 18, 32, 55, 95, 155,
  245, 375, 560, 805
)
# Generate scatter plot
plot(
  temperature,
  pressure,
  main = "Temperature vs Pressure",
  xlab = "temperature",
  ylab = "pressure",
  pch = 1
)

```

Note that the echo = FALSE parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.


Understanding the plot() function



temperature: Data for the X-axis

pressure : Data for the Y-axis

main: Graph title

xlab: X-axis label

ylab: X-asis label

pch = 1 : Displays hollow circular points



You can customize the graph using:

pch = 19: Solid circles.

col = "blue": Blue points.

cex = 1.2: Increases point size.

Create a vector with NAs in it


Return a logical vector on which elements is na

```{r}

```

```{r}
x <-c(1,2,3,NA, 5)
```


What if there are multiple R objects and you want to take the subset with no missing values of those objects?

```{r}

good
```

## Coercion in R

Coercion means converting a value from one data type to another data type.

For example , R may convert number into characters or logical values into numbers when different type of data are combined


Example 1: Automatic coercion

```{r}
 # Although most values are numbers, "three" is a character. R converts all values to characters:
x <-c(1,2,"three", 4)
x
```

Example 2: Coercion hierarchy

A common coercion order in R is:

logical -> integer -> numeric -> character

```{r}

y<-c(TRUE, 2, 2.5, "Hello")

# The result becomes a character vector:
y
```

Example 3: Explicit coercion

You can manually convert data using  functions such as:
```{r}
as.numeric("25")
```

```{r}
as.numeric("Hello")
```

If a vector only contains logical and numbers, R will convert the logical to numbers, Every true becomes a 1, and every FALSE becomes 0

```{r}
sum(c(TRUE,TRUE,FALSE,FALSE,FALSE))
```

## Understanding apply()

The apply() function is used to perform a function across the rows or columns of a matrix or array.

General syntax:

apply(X, MARGIN, FUN)

X	Dataset or matrix
MARGIN	Specifies rows or columns
FUN	Function to apply

### Understanding 1 and 2

This is very important:
  1 = Apply the function across rows.
  2 = Apply the function across columns.


Example using your HEIGHT and WEIGHT dataset

Suppose your data looks like this:

HEIGHT	WEIGHT

175	72

162	56

180	81

158	52

170	68

Calculate the mean of each row:

```{r}
data_class_mean <- apply(data_class, 1, mean)
data_class_mean
```

Calculation:

Row	Calculation	Mean

1	(175 + 72) / 2	123.5

2	(162 + 56) / 2	109

3	(180 + 81) / 2	130.5

4	(158 + 52) / 2	105

5	(170 + 68) / 2	119


Calculate the mean of each column:

```{r}

# This calculates:
#- Average HEIGHT.
#- Average WEIGHT.

apply(data_class, 2, mean)

```
Other examples of apply()
```{r}
# Calculate sum of each row
apply(data_class, 1, sum)

# Calculate sum of each column
apply(data_class, 2, sum)

# Find maximum value in each column
apply(data_class, 2, max)

# Find minimum value in each column
apply(data_class, 2, min)

# Calculate standard deviation of each column
apply(data_class, 2, sd)
```

Rows : apply(data_class, 1, mean) 

Calculates the mean of each row.

Columns : apply(data_class, 2, mean)

Calculates the mean of each column.


```{r}
c(mean(data_class$HEIGHT),sd(data_class$HEIGHT))
```


```{r}
c(mean(data_class$WEIGHT),sd(data_class$WEIGHT))
```
```{r}
c(Mean=mean(data_class$HEIGHT),SD=sd(data_class$HEIGHT))
```

```{r}
c(Mean=mean(data_class$WEIGHT),SD=sd(data_class$WEIGHT))
```

## Visualize the differences in continuous variables between categories using Box-and-whisker plot

comparing the quantitative variable Sepal.Length across the categorical variable Species in the built-in iris dataset.


Component	         Explanation

boxplot()	         Creates a box-and-whisker plot.
iris$Sepal.Length	 Quantitative variable (numerical data).
iris$Species	     Categorical variable (setosa, versicolor, virginica).
~	                 Separates the quantitative variable from the grouping variable.
data =             iris	Specifies the dataset.
main	             Defines the chart title.


```{r}
boxplot(iris$Sepal.Length~iris$Species,data=iris, main="Comparison of categorical vs quantitative")
```

You can make the visualization clearer by adding axis labels and colors.

```{r}

boxplot(iris$Sepal.Length~iris$Species, data=iris, main="Comparison of categorical vs quantitative",
        xlab = "Iris Speciies", ylab = "Iris Sepal Length cm",
        col=c("lightblue","lightgreen","lightpink"),
        border="black"
)
```

## Simpson’s paradox

Phenomenon, where a trend that appears in combined groups of data disappears or reverses when broken down into groups.

```{r}
cross2<-xtabs(Freq~Gender+Admit,data=ucba[ucba$Dept=="F",])
prop.table(cross2,1)
```

## Subsetting

Use of $, []. or [[]]
Creation of leadership data Interest: How men and women differ in the way they lead their organizations. 5 questions were asked in this study. Example of the question: Do men and women in management position differ in the degree to which they defer to superiors? 1: strongly disagree, 2: disagree, 3:neither agree nor disagree,4: agree, 5: strongly agree

```{r}

manager <- c(1,2,3,4,5)
country<- c("US","US","UK","UK","UK")
gender<-c("M","F","F","M","F")
age<-c(32,45,25,39,99)
q1<-c(5,3,3,3,2)
q2<-c(4,5,5,3,2)
q3<-c(5,2,5,4,1)
q4<-c(5,5,5,NA,2)
q5<-c(5,5,2,NA,1)
leadership<-data.frame(manager,country, gender, age, q1,q2,q3,q4,q5, stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
leadership<-data.frame(manager,country, gender, age, q1,q2,q3,q4,q5)

str(leadership)


```

```{r}
names(leadership)
```

What you can do - combine the score of the five questions -handle the missing values - create a dataset of what you want -create age group or age categories - 99 indicate the value is missing


## Missing value
```{r}
leadership$age[leadership$age==99]<-NA
View(leadership)
```


```{r}

leadership$agecat[leadership$age >75]<-"Elder"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age>=35 & leadership$age<=75]<-"Middle Aged"
leadership$agecat[leadership$age <35]<- "Young"
leadership
```

### One way to handle missing value

Deleting all observations with missing data ( Listwise deletion) is one of the several methods of handling incomplete datasets. Note: You can also replacing the missing value by the average of the remaining data.

```{r}
is.na(leadership[,5:9])
```
Removes all rows containing at least one missing value (NA) from the leadership dataset.

```{r}
newdata<-na.omit(leadership)
newdata
```

```{r}
newdata2
```

## Merging data sets

To merge two data frame horizontally, you use merge() function. In most cases, two data frames are joined by one or more common key variables. -example 1: merge(dataframeA, dataframeB,by=“ID”) -example 2: merge(dataframeA,dataframeB, by=c(“ID”,“country”))

the second merge the two dataframes by ID and country

To join two data frame( datasets) vertically, use rbind() function: Note that the two data set must have the same variables

### Subset (selecting variables,dropping variables,selecting observation )

```{r}
newdata3<-leadership[,c(5:9)]
myvars<-c("q1","q2","q3","q4","q5")
(newdata3<-leadership[myvars])
```

```{r}
newdata4<-leadership[,c(-1,-2)]
(newdata4<-leadership[,-(1:5)]) # exclude columns from 1 to 5
```


```{r}
newdata5<-leadership[,c(-1,-7)]
leadership[[4]]
```

```{r}
leadership$age
```

```{r}
newdata6<-leadership[c(-1,-3),]
newdata6<-leadership[c(2,4,5),]
newdata7<-subset(leadership,age>=35|age<24,select=c(q1,q2,q3,q4,q5))
```
